articles.text: General Grant is pronounced by his doctors, to be better than he has been for two months past.
articles.summary: Brief on Gen. Grant's health.

articles.text: Major Carland of Bismarck, has been appointed United States attorney, and Morris Taylor, surveyor general.
articles.summary: Territorial appointments of Carland and Taylor.

articles.text: The recent warm rains have sent the grass up a foot high. Feed could not possibly be better than it is now.
articles.summary: Rains have brought the range grass up a foot.

articles.text: President Cleveland is manifesting a disposition to appoint residents of Dakota to Territorial offices instead of inflicting "carpet baggers" upon us.
articles.summary: Cleveland favoring Dakota residents for territorial offices.

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt has the material of a first-class candidate for Governor in him, but he, too, will probably have to wait till his beard is longer. Yet he holds a pretty lofty seat in the Republican synagogue already, and he has got it by his own abilities without any outside help Roosevelt is no slouch as a public man, and don't you forget it.—[New York Sun.
articles.summary: New York Sun praise of Roosevelt as future gubernatorial material, reprinted.

articles.text: Kaolin was discovered by John Fredrick Bottgher in the year 1707. He had for years experimenting with different kinds of clay to make white porcelain and finally stumbled on to the right thing by accident. One day he found his perruque unusually heavy, and upon investigation found the cause to be the unusual quantity of white clay used in the hair powder, and which he found upon experiment to be kaolin, from which he produced the first piece of porcelain in October 1707.
articles.summary: Anecdote on the discovery of kaolin (porcelain clay).

articles.text:
It is reported that the Dominion government, in settling with the families of soldiers who have been killed in the war up in the northwest, deduct the amount paid out for funeral expenses. If this is a fact, the Dominion authorities ought to get the premium for meanness.—[Bismarck Tribune.

It is undoubtedly a fact that a government capable of prosecuting such a war on its own subjects, is perfectly competent to rob its soldiers' widows, and orphans. Next.
articles.summary: Bismarck Tribune item on Canada deducting funeral costs from soldiers' families, with Cow Boy comment.

articles.text: In our next issue, will begin the true history of the Lost Cabin mining claim. The location of which, it has been generally thought, was in the Big Horn mountains, but this history will prove that blief to have been erroneous. The account is by an old miner, now living in Medora, and who is a nephew of the original discoverer of the mine. It is not improbable that a prospecting party will outfit here this summer and make an attempt to find the Lost Cabin, where untold wealth is waiting the lucky finder. If a party is organized it will be for a two years trip.
articles.summary: Announces a coming serial history of the Lost Cabin mine by a Medora miner.

articles.text: The Deadwood Times of the 18th., says, work will begin on the Deadwood & Redwater R. R. about June 1st. Grade and slope stakes have been set for 25 miles on the northern terminus. The road will have a total length of 50 miles, reaching Centennial through False Bottom, traversing Centennial to the mouth of Whitewood Canyon, thence to Deadwood. It will be narrow gauge and constructed in the most substantial manner at an estimated cost of $500,000. Representatives of the syndicate who are furnishing the capital are on the road to the Hills for the purpose of letting contracts for grading, ties, bridge-building, &c.
articles.summary: Deadwood & Redwater narrow-gauge railroad to begin work June 1.

articles.text: The Butcher and Drover, a Philadelphia paper and the Drovers Journal, of Chicago are having a "set-to" over the condition of cattle that are slaughtered at the abbatoirs in their respective cities. The Philadelphia paper says, "the board of health should appoint a committee to investigate the quality of the western dressed beeves that are sold in this city, as well as all the maimed and sick cattle that are brought from the far west and killed at Chicago, embalmed and sent here for our people to eat." The Chicago paper in reply says, "our health agent says this is an insulting lie." "Go it old man, go it bear," and Medora will kill beef on the range, where it does not get sick or crippled, and supply both your cities.
articles.summary: Comment on Philadelphia-Chicago press quarrel over dressed beef, boosting Medora beef.

articles.text: W. J. Tompkins is the pioneer in a new branch of industry in the Little Missouri valley. He outfitted here Monday morning with the necessary implements to start a hay ranch which will be located about 15 miles from town. About one hundred acres will be broken and seeded this year. Experiments will be made with alfalfa, red clover, timothy, millet, &c. This new enterprise will without doubt be successful and will be of great advantage to our stockmen. It is a well known fact that the native grasses will yield a crop of hay only once in about every two or three years, and in addition to this, the country is filling up so rapidly with stock that even this supply will be entirely cut off within the next two or three years. The Refrigerator company expects to feed cattle here through the winter and must look for their supplies, to some other source than the native meadows. It is claimed that cattle fed on alfalfa will not only retain their flesh, but will take on more. This hay business is a matter that should be looked into by stockmen, as there is a possibility that they will need hay when there is none to be obtained.
articles.summary: W. J. Tompkins starts a hay ranch 15 miles from Medora.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES.
articles.text:
Annoncement.

Cattle-men of the Little Missouri river are advised that the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, will give them during June for the beef and dry cows that they wish to sell, Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred to cover freight and shrinkage. The cattle to be delivered in the evening at the Sully Creek corrals and weighed in the morning.

Marquis de Mores,
President.
articles.summary: De Mores announces N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. will buy beef and dry cows in June at Chicago prices less 70 cents.

articles.text: Our Aurora correspondent is informed that millet is a heavy producer. Just how much could be produced would depend, of course, upon the character of the soil. It makes a superior fodder for cattle if cut before it is ripe. The ground should be plowed the ordinary depth for this crop. Sow from sixteen to twenty quarts to the acre. Sow the last of May.—[Am. Stockman.

articles.text: Good horses are bringing better prices in all parts of the country than they have commanded since the war, and poor horses were never so unsalable as compared with the best as they are to-day. A farmer who breeds a good mare to a good horse will have a sure and profitable market for his colt. There can be no profit in breeding to common stock. Select the best stallions, those that are surest, and having size, form and action. It will cost a little more for the service, but it will pay to breed to the best.—[R. M. Husbandman.
articles.summary: Clipped advice on horse breeding.

articles.text: The Continental and Hash Knife cattle companies have recently made an important sale of 35,000 head of stock cattle at $17.50 around to the Aztec Land & cattle Co. This purchase includes all stock cattle belonging to these companies below the New Mexico line on Pecos river excluding beeves and twos. The Aztec company is composed of heavy New York capitalists and is the largest in the southwest. Their investment including one million acres of railroad land on the Atlantic and Pacific road in Apache county, Arizona, already aggregates over $1.500.000 in land and cattle. The cattle purchased are of a high grade and make an excellent foundation for such a largo outfit.
articles.summary: Sale of 35,000 cattle by Continental and Hash Knife companies to the Aztec Land & Cattle Co.

articles.text: The St Paul Globe says, "no cattle have been quarantined on the Montana border. The Frye cattle were taken off the cars by their owner to be branded and grazed before being taken on their range near Billings." It is to be hoped that the Globe is not so much of a "tenderfoot" as it is trying to make itself out to be. The fact is well known that these cattle were turned loose on the prairie at Sentinel Butte, Mont., where there are no yards, much less a branding chute, and that the owner had neither horses or men at hand to hold the cattle after they were unloaded from the cars. It might be well for the Globe man to "go west" and try to learn a little about handling cattle before attempting to gloss over some body's sculldugery.
articles.summary: Cow Boy disputes St. Paul Globe on the Frye cattle unloaded at Sentinel Butte.

articles.text: The adjutant-general of Texas, is in receipt of information that 6,000 heed of cattle, purchased in south Texas by Abner, Taylor & Co., and now enroute to their Daltam county ranch, have been stopped at Harrold, Wichita county, by the north Texas cattlemen and forbidden to proceed further. Those having the cattle in charge applied to a company of rangers, located near Harrold for protection, alleging that armed men would resist their passage through the country. The rangers telegraphed to the adjutant-general for instructions to-day, and were ordered to respond promptly to any call made upon them by the civil authorities, to whom the men in charge of the cattle were referred for aid and assistance. If they refused or failed, the government will invoke the military of the state. Bloodshed and trouble is anticipated when the drive is attempted.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Texas drive of 6,000 cattle stopped at Harrold by north Texas cattlemen.

articles.headline: THE NEW TRAIL
articles.text:
"The question of a public trail through the Texas Panhandle, which has been agitating the minds of the ranchmen for some time, has been solved to the satisfaction of southern cattlemen, if not to the Panhandle men. From H. W. Cresswell, of Ft. Elliott, Texas, The Indicator learns that while there is considerable dissatisfaction in regard to the location of the trail, it is generally conceded the route selected will work the least possible injury to the Panhandle cattlemen." * * * The new trail as projected is laid out as follows. "Leaving the old Ft. Griffin and Dodge trail, at 16-Mile creek, the trail runs westward 20 miles to Clear creek, thence 16 miles to Kiowa, thence 18 miles to Clear, thence 20 miles to Fulton, thence 15 miles to the rifle-pits on Palo Duro, thence 20 miles to Coldwater, thence 8 miles to second water on Coldwater, thence 35 miles to Buffalo Springs, thence in a northwest direction through the Neutral Strip to the mouth of the Carizzo, near the Colorado line." **

A meeting was held at Dallas, Texas last week which was attended by nearly a hundred representative ranchmen, including members of the executive committees of the various [local?] associations. At this meeting, Col. Simpson expressed the opinion that if an outlet through the northwestern part of Texas, was not given, the stockmen would without doubt make one for themselves. It was intimated by some one that Gov. Ireland had as much as said that he would call on the rangers to assist them.

"Continuing, Col. Simpson said that what they wanted was harmony, and if possible, a cattle trail. There was likely to be, if the matter was not satisfactorily adjusted, trouble, and the cow-boys did not mind a little loss of blood occasionally, but they were rather sensitive when it came to touching their pocket-books. They were good men, and looked after their own interest. The cattleman in the eyes of the law had a right to drive over the highway to effect an outlet, and the live stock interest of the State depended largely upon the action of the meeting they were holding. He closed by advising calm, dispassionate deliberation, with fair play as the watchword. President Simpson parenthetically remarked that one of the most important questions which would come up for consideration, was the stopping of the shipments of cattle of the cattle syndicate by the Panhandle association. These were en route to Dallam county, and had been stopped at Harrold." * * *

A conference committee of five members from northwest Texas was appointed to report on the proposed new trail. The committee all signed a report in favor of the trail, with the exception of W. A. Towers who explained his position to be due to instructions from his association. The following resolution was unanimously adopted as the final sense of the convention."

1. Believing that a trail should be established in some legal manner, it is the sense of this convention that the State should, in some way provide such a trail, and we pledge ourselves to use means in our power to bring about in some way such legislation as may be necessary to secure such a State trail.

2. That a committee of three be appointed by the chair to present the matter to the governor.

Messrs. O. H. Nelson, H. W. Cresswell, and J. R. Hamilton were appointed as such committee."
articles.summary: Report on the proposed public cattle trail through the Texas Panhandle and the Dallas ranchmen's meeting.

articles.text: Hotel DeBoyd will open up June 1st.
articles.summary: Hotel DeBoyd to open June 1.

articles.text: Howard Eaton was in town yesterday.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton in town.

articles.text: J. A. McGregor and wife are in from the ranch.
articles.summary: McGregors in from the ranch.

articles.text: John Munro left for Bismarck yesterday morning.
articles.summary: Munro leaves for Bismarck.

articles.text: J. A. Ferris has just received a new stock of hats.
articles.summary: Ferris receives new hats.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts will depart for the east in a few days after more cattle.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts going east for cattle.

articles.text: The country about Dickinson was visited by a severe hail-storm last week.
articles.summary: Hail storm near Dickinson.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock left for Deadwood last Friday, will be absent about eight days.
articles.summary: Paddock to Deadwood.

articles.text: Frank D. Foster superintendent of the slaughter-house, returned last Saturday bringing his family with him.
articles.summary: Foster returns with family.

articles.text: Rev. Father Martin will hold services in the church Sunday morning at nine o'clock. All are specially invited.
articles.summary: Catholic service Sunday.

articles.text: Nine butchers arrived from Chicago Friday evening. They will all be employed in the new slaughter-house.
articles.summary: Nine Chicago butchers arrive for slaughter-house.

articles.text: A full line of mirrors, glassware, crockery, lamps and fixtures, at the drug store. Latest styles and patterns.
articles.summary: Drug store advertises glassware and lamps.

articles.text: Geo. Fitzgerald, John Kiefer and Bob. Roberts have been subpoenaed as witnesses in Wm. Roberts trial at Miles City.
articles.summary: Medora men subpoenaed for Roberts trial.

articles.text: McKenzie & O'brien have moved their blacksmith shop to the north side of the track and are now ready for business again.
articles.summary: Blacksmiths move north of the track.

articles.text: Tramps are again becoming numerous in town. Where is our "fireing" committee? Come genttleman get to the front.
articles.summary: Complaint of tramps in town.

articles.text: Messrs Grymes and Lozier brought in a fine specimen of wild brant last Sunday, consisting of a hen and seven chicks.
articles.summary: Grymes and Lozier bring in wild brant.

articles.text: Still a few of our citizens are "short" on backyard "cleanups." Where is our "garbage" committee? probably not dead but sleeping.
articles.summary: Complaint about backyard garbage.

articles.text: The Dominion government is still as much at a loss what to do with Riel as the Marquis was what use to make out of the "Black Maria."
articles.summary: Quip comparing Riel's fate with de Mores and the "Black Maria."

articles.text: Bob Roberts has just returned from Miles City and he says all the buildings that are left there since the fire, wouldn't make a decent suburbs for Medora.
articles.summary: Roberts back from fire-damaged Miles City.

articles.text: If any one wants a muss on their hands (right smart,) just ask Mr. Turkey Bill if he is from Chicago. Take off that dude collar Bill so that your friends will know you.
articles.summary: Jibe at "Turkey Bill."

articles.text: The cow outfits from this part of the country started from the logging camp last Saturday for the mouth of Box Elder where the general round-up work was began on Monday.
articles.summary: Outfits leave for the general round-up at Box Elder.

articles.text: B. Barr made his friends a two days visit last week, returning to his home in Kansas City on Monday morning. He will possibly make us another visit this fall with a drive of cattle.
articles.summary: B. Barr visits from Kansas City.

articles.text: I respectfully inform all who want first class Tonsorial work done, that I am now running a first class Barber shop and am prepared to accommodate all callers. Fred. Banan.
articles.summary: Fred Banan opens barber shop.

articles.text: Hizoner, J. S. Warn returned to his home and friends in Medora last Friday. He will soon enlarge his restaurant and make the Oyster Grotto the best place in the northwest to get a good square meal.
articles.summary: Warn returns, will enlarge Oyster Grotto.

articles.text: Fred Watson has started in to paint the west side a violent carmine hue, beginning with the front of his feed stable. Fred is doing a rushing business, and gives a good square feed every time.
articles.summary: Watson paints his feed stable.

articles.text: Pete Book went to Miles City last night to put in bids on brick to be furnished for the new syndicate block to be built there. If quality and price are any object, Pete will get the contract.
articles.summary: Pete Book bids on Miles City brick contract.

articles.text: The improvements at the Coal mine are completed and everything is in fine running order. A new chute has been made, a track laid and buggy placed on it, and an air shaft sunk to give thorough ventilation.
articles.summary: Coal mine improvements completed.

articles.text: What has become of the Medora Rifle Club? Have they crawled into their holes and died? Would it not be well to call a meeting of the Club and declare the last contest closed and make the award of the rifle to the winner.
articles.summary: Query on the Medora Rifle Club.

articles.text: Two mongolians visited our city on Sunday morning, but left on the next train, having concluded that the climate was too severe to insure them good health. If the "climate" had been less impregnated with "bug-juice" it would have undoubtedly been more congenial.
articles.summary: Two Chinese visitors leave town on the next train.

articles.text: N. G. Dakin of LaPorte, Ind., returning from a trip to Portland, Oregon., made us a pleasant call on last Sunday. He reports stock looking well all along the line. He is well pleased with this country and will probably return at no distant day to make his home in the northwest.
articles.summary: N. G. Dakin calls at the Cow Boy.

articles.text:
Two ex-Medora stage employes were run in by Officer Duffy last evening for disorderly conduct on Main street. They will have a hearing today.—[Deadwood Times.

So thats what kept you so long in Deadwood was it boys. John and William are generally pretty good boys at home.
articles.summary: Two former Medora stage employees arrested in Deadwood.

articles.text:
"Some body's looking, love,
Pull down the blinds."

That's what she said last Sunday when the young man had his arm around her up on the "butte farm." Young folks, let me put a flea in your ear. Don't get spooney over on the west side, for Fred. has an Eagle eye for all such business.
articles.summary: Teasing item about a courting couple on the "butte farm."

articles.text: Truscott went east a few days ago and now Pack'., has gone east. What does it all mean anyway? Is there method in this madness? It is supposed to be catching but not contagious. "If so be" that it is, "good Lord deliver us."
articles.summary: Truscott and Packard both gone east.

articles.text: Have you heard the latest? Pete, the amphibious manipulator of Tantalus' cup, astutely refused a drink this morning. "No sah, hasn't got time dis mawnin." Pete wears the white apron at the new brick hotel and means to hold it down. Stay with it Pete.
articles.summary: Bartender Pete at the new brick hotel refuses a drink.

articles.text: The new Engine at the slaughter-house turned the first wheel this morning. Everything moved as smooth as if it had been running six months. The Engine is of the Buckeye pattern. It was selected by Mr. Wilkes and has several improvements suggested by himself. She is a daisy George and beats "the bat" by several degrees.
articles.summary: New Buckeye engine starts at the slaughter-house.

articles.text: It is rumored that the Hon. Theo. Roosevelt, D. K. Wade and others, have begun permanent improvements in the region near the "logging camp." The excavations for artificial lakes, and fountains have been begun. It is also intimated that electric lights will be supplied from the electricity, profanity &c that was collected and bottled up at the time of embarkation for the round-up.
articles.summary: Joking rumor of Roosevelt and Wade "improvements" near the logging camp.

articles.text:
Fannie Field says in the Prairie Farmer as to roosters: "Do not overdo the rooster business. Too many roosters in one flock are as bad as not enough; in fact, too much rooster is worse than not enough, for in the latter case more of the eggs will be fertile, but in the former, the hens are so worried by the everlasting attention of the males of the flock that they become disgusted and dodge them altogether." * * *

Well Fannie, we agree with you in this matter. What we need, is more hens. We are not overstocked with roosters in this country but are terribly short of hens.
articles.summary: Joke on a Prairie Farmer poultry tip: the country is short of hens (women).

articles.text:
John Gaston has received the appointment as agent for the Miles City buckboard line. It is to hoped that he will bring about an improvement in the operation thereof.—[B. H. Times.

Gaston is bound to run a stage line to the Northern Pacific if it takes all summer. Stay with it John, we will bet on you everytime to rake in the persimmons. We rather look to see the Medora line running again before long but hope it will not be done by an outfit who will be tenderfoot enough to place any reliance on the statements of Deadwood merchants.
articles.summary: John Gaston named agent for the Miles City buckboard line; hopes for revival of Medora stage line.

articles.headline: LIGHTNING.
articles.text:
Marquis de Mores Residence in Medora the Victim.

A severe thunder storm visited this section last Wednesday afternoon. The lightning struck a chimney on the residence ofthe Marquis and ran down to the water pipe leading to the well. The rooms through which the electric fluid passed, were pretty badly demoralized. Plastering torn off, mirrors broken and a large hole knocked in the outer wall. Several people were standing near the chimney when the lightning struck and were all more or less shocked. As the colored lady remarked, "da was all knocked clar sensible." Mr. Day who was doing some painting in the room where the chimney was, endeavored to capture some of the festive fluid, but succeeded only in leaving the marks of his fingers on the wall. He also assumed a recumbent position and gazed upon the azure sky above him, through the hole in the roof. Happily, no one was injured, aud on extensive damage done.
articles.summary: Lightning strikes the Marquis de Mores' residence in Medora.

events.excerpt: We don't propose to come here for a few days. We are here to stay.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 28 May 1885 issue
events.title: Carland named U.S. attorney and Taylor surveyor general for Dakota
events.summary: The Cow Boy noted that Major Carland of Bismarck had been appointed United States attorney and Morris Taylor surveyor general.
events.excerpt: Major Carland of Bismarck, has been appointed United States attorney, and Morris Taylor, surveyor general.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 28 May 1885 issue
events.title: Warm rains bring range grass up a foot high
events.summary: The paper reported that recent warm rains had sent the grass up a foot high and that feed could not be better.
events.excerpt: The recent warm rains have sent the grass up a foot high.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 28 May 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy reprints New York Sun: Roosevelt has the makings of a governor
events.summary: The Cow Boy reprinted a New York Sun paragraph saying Theodore Roosevelt had the material of a first-class candidate for Governor but would probably have to wait until he was older.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt has the material of a first-class candidate for Governor in him, but he, too, will probably have to wait till his beard is longer.

events.date_basis: "In our next issue" after Thu 28 May 1885

events.summary: The paper announced it would begin, in its next issue, a history of the Lost Cabin mining claim told by an old miner living in Medora, a nephew of the discoverer, and said a prospecting party might outfit at Medora that summer.
events.excerpt: The account is by an old miner, now living in Medora, and who is a nephew of the original discoverer of the mine.

events.date_basis: "about June 1st" per Deadwood Times of 18 May 1885
events.title: Work to begin on the Deadwood & Redwater railroad
events.summary: Quoting the Deadwood Times, the paper reported that work on the 50-mile narrow-gauge Deadwood & Redwater railroad would begin about June 1, at an estimated cost of $500,000.
events.excerpt: work will begin on the Deadwood & Redwater R. R. about June 1st.

events.date_basis: "Monday morning" before Thu 28 May 1885
events.title: W. J. Tompkins outfits at Medora to start a hay ranch
events.summary: W. J. Tompkins outfitted at Medora to start a hay ranch about 15 miles from town, planning to break and seed about 100 acres with alfalfa, clover, timothy and millet; the paper noted the Refrigerator company expected to winter-feed cattle.
events.excerpt: He outfitted here Monday morning with the necessary implements to start a hay ranch which will be located about 15 miles from town.

events.date_basis: "during June" per announcement in Thu 28 May 1885 issue
events.title: De Mores offers Chicago prices for Little Missouri beef in June
events.summary: The Marquis de Mores, as president of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, announced the company would buy beef and dry cows from Little Missouri cattlemen during June at Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred, delivered at the Sully Creek corrals.
events.excerpt: will give them during June for the beef and dry cows that they wish to sell, Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred

events.excerpt: From Custer Trail Ranch about April 1st., a red or strawberry roan pony seven or eight years old

events.excerpt: these cattle were turned loose on the prairie at Sentinel Butte, Mont., where there are no yards, much less a branding chute

events.excerpt: Two ex-Medora stage employes were run in by Officer Duffy last evening for disorderly conduct on Main street.

events.date_basis: "For week ending May 27"

events.excerpt: Greatest rainfall at one time, 1¼ inch on the 27. accompanyed with heavy thunder.

events.date_basis: "Saturday night" after Thu 28 May 1885
